rows.reviewerNote: Judged as a new question against lines 3 and 4. 'Grows bigger and takes up more room.' is the only meaning the lines support for 'Wood swells': the doors stop shutting. 'Rises louder' and 'Grows in number' are genuine senses the context rules out decisively, because wood cannot grow louder or more numerous. 'Stops sitting flat in its frame' is the result, not the meaning. There is no echo of the stem. The shared opening 'Grows' with C is not a cue, and lengths run 6 to 8 words. Annie's hint names no option. The walk states the key.

changes.before: Line 3 has him say the door is swollen. Line 3 says wood swells. Line 3 says one hot summer does it.
changes.after: Line 3 has him say the door is swollen, and that wood swells. Lines 3 and 4 say one hot summer stops every door shutting properly. So swells means the wood grows bigger and takes up more room.
Line 3 has him say the door is swollen. Line 3 says wood swells. Line 3 says one hot summer does it.

changes.before: Gets bigger as it takes in the heat.
changes.after: Grows bigger and takes up more room.

changes.before: True at line 4, and it is what follows rather than the word.
changes.after: Lines 3 and 4 say every door 'stops shutting properly' once the wood swells. The child takes that result, a door that no longer sits right in its frame, for what the word means.

rows.reviewerNote: Judged as a new question against lines 33 and 34. The key matches line 33 ('in the Friday box, low down') and line 34 ('pushed it flat'), and it is the only correct option. The returns box is contradicted by line 33. The bin bag reuses lines 29 and 30. Folding and giving the jumper to Miss Bhatt belongs to lines 48 and 49. There is no near-identical pair. The two 'because' options are both decoys, but the key shares its action form with D, so form does not single out the key. The hint sends the child to the sentence starting on line 33, which is exact. The walk states the key.

changes.before: Put it in the Friday box, low down, and pressed it flat.
changes.after: Put it in the Friday box, low down, and pushed it flat.

changes.before: Put it in the returns box, low down, and pushed it flat.
changes.after: Put it in the returns box, because his name was in it.

changes.before: Line 33 says he put it 'in the Friday box, low down', the box going to the charity collection, and line 34 that he 'pushed it flat'. The child keeps how he did it and changes the box to the returns box, which named things go in at lines 7 and 8 and which the passage says he did not use here.
changes.after: Lines 7 and 8 send named things to the returns box, and line 46 shows the jumper has his name in it. But line 33 says he put it 'in the Friday box, low down', the box going to the charity collection.

rows.reviewerNote: Judged as a new question against lines 43 and 44, and line 33 for the stacking. 'A level of things lying on others.' is the only sense that fits lifting the top layer of clothes out of a box to reach the jumper beneath. A coat of paint or dust and a laying hen are real senses that the box rules out, and no list exists. The echo of 'top' is gone, and lengths run 5 to 8 words. The hint names no option. The walk ends on the key.

changes.before: Look at lines 43 and 44. She lifts the top layer out and keeps going down. Under it she reaches the navy jumper. So a layer here is the things lying on top.
changes.after: Look at lines 43 and 44. She lifts the top layer out and keeps going down. Under it she reaches the navy jumper. So a layer here is a level of things lying on others.
Look at lines 43 and 44. She lifts the top layer out and keeps going down. Under it she reaches the navy jumper. So a layer here is the things lying on top.

changes.before: The things lying across the top.
changes.after: A level of things lying on others.

rows.reviewerNote: Checked against lines 37 to 40, and line 2 for C. The key is lines 39 and 40, and it is the only answer to what happens both times. rows.reviewerNote: Checked across the whole passage. The remarks at lines 11, 13, 14 and 15 each notice a difference from the King, and he calls them 'mere flattery' (line 16) and 'signs of approval' (line 17). That makes the key the only reading. C asserts a remark he never makes. B has no line giving fear. A is two moments (lines 6 and 17). The walk now reaches lines 16 and 17 and states the key, with every sentence 16 words or fewer.

changes.before: Line 11 says he looks paler than usual. Line 13 says he is bigger than they thought. Line 14 says he had a good jaw under the beard.
changes.after: Line 11 says he looks paler than usual. Line 13 says he is bigger than they thought. Line 14 says he had a good jaw under the beard. Line 16 calls one remark mere flattery. Line 17 calls the remarks signs of approval. So they keep on noticing the difference, but what he hears in it is approval.
Line 11 says he looks paler than usual. Line 13 says he is bigger than they thought. Line 14 says he had a good jaw under the beard.

rows.reviewerNote: Checked against lines 1 to 4. The key is line 4 ('admit that I made a very fine figure'), and it is the only admission. The white clothes at line 1 are what he wore, not the admission. 'doing the King little credit' comes from dropping 'if I did not' on line 3. The preparation option has no line behind it. Lengths run 7 to 11 words, with no echo and no twin. The hint and walk script are unchanged, and the walk states the key at line 4.

changes.after: Line 3 says he would pay the King a poor compliment only 'if I did not set modesty aside'. The child drops 'if I did not' and reads it as something he admits: that he does the King little credit.

changes.after: A man doing this once invites preparation; no line gives any. Lines 3 and 4 have him admit only that he made a very fine figure.

rows.reviewerNote: Checked against lines 36 to 40. The key is line 39 ('that will be about the fountain, and the fountain was ages ago'), and it is the only explanation the lines give him. Each distractor is wrong: the mother's early arrival is line 36, no promise is given (lines 36 and 37 give only 'a small nod'), and 'just what she is saying' explains nothing. All four begin 'That', with lengths 11 to 13 words. The hint and walk are unchanged and still accurate. Note for a later pass: the walk's 'say the word again' is unquoted and could read as 'say it a second time'.

changes.after: That it is about his mother coming in early, at half past two.

rows.reviewerNote: Checked against lines 6 to 9 and 60 to 63. The key holds: the crowd checks his hair (lines 8 and 9) and nobody dreams he could be anyone else (lines 62 and 63).
